$about: The brand interview. One question at a time; every answer carries a status and a source. Emits brand.md + brand.json.
title: Brand interview

sections.title: Evidence
sections.note: What this brand is, and what you actually read before answering.

sections.title: Define
sections.note: What exists today. Facts, not ambition.

sections.title: Position
sections.note: What you claim, and what you can prove.

sections.title: Operate
sections.note: How it sounds, what it costs, what moves next.

sections.title: Identity
sections.note: The visual system: colour roles, type roles, imagery, motion, forbidden territory.

sections.title: Direction
sections.note: Where the brand should go next, as decisions rather than adjectives.

questions.label: Product
questions.question: What is this brand called, and what is it?
questions.help: The name as it would appear on the door.
questions.why: Every later slot references this name — the record title, the browser tab, the first headline. It must be unambiguous, including spelling and capitalisation.
questions.example: Beagles Bikes — not BeeGles, not beagles bikes. Write it the way you want to read it back.

questions.label: One line
questions.question: In one line, what is it?
questions.help: One sentence, under 25 words, that a stranger understands on first read.
questions.placeholder: A personal digital garden of writing, photography and small signals.
questions.why: This line becomes the record hero and the shorthand every later answer is measured against. If it cannot be said in one breath, the site cannot either.
questions.example: A friendly bicycle repair workshop that collects and returns your bike in under 48 hours.

questions.label: Stage
questions.question: Where is it now?
questions.help: Where the business is today. Be honest — pre-launch is a normal answer, not a failure.
questions.why: It decides what "proof" can mean later: a pre-launch brand proves intent and assets; a live one proves numbers and customers.
questions.example: Pre-launch (workshop fitted, no site yet) · Trading 3 months · Trading 2 years + rebrand.
questions.tbcHint: Between stages? Pick the one that describes most of this month, not most of the plan.

questions.label: Owner and date
questions.question: Who owns this record, and when was it last verified?
questions.help: Who maintains this record, and when was it last checked against reality.
questions.why: A brand record drifts. Named ownership and a date make the next agent treat stale slots as stale rather than as truth.
questions.example: Sulei — last verified 2026-10-29 after the shop sign was fitted.
questions.tbcHint: Solo? Still write your own name. "Not stated" gets flagged as a gap later.

questions.label: Sources read
questions.question: What did you actually read to fill this in?
questions.help: What you actually read or did before answering anything else — files, URLs, conversations.
questions.placeholder:
design.md
tokens.json
https://example.com/
Two customer calls, 14 Oct
questions.why: Every "Verified" status elsewhere is anchored here. No sources listed means the record must downgrade those claims to assumptions.
questions.example: Shop premises lease (a real document) · three customer conversations · competitor sites read on 28 Oct.
questions.tbcHint: Answered nothing on evidence? List the one conversation you have already had, or mark TBC — the gap table will carry it.

questions.label: A1 The thing
questions.question: What is it, in one sentence a customer would repeat to a friend?
questions.help: Under 20 words. No category jargon. Name the outcome, not the mechanism.
questions.why: This becomes the hero sentence of the site. Over 20 words, or naming a mechanism, and the headline has to invent a translation.
questions.example: Bike hire and a repair workshop that comes to your door. — outcome first, mechanism second, under 20 words.

questions.label: A2 Who
questions.question: Who buys, who uses, and who pays — and are they the same person?
questions.help: A named segment with a size you can count, a place they gather, and what they already spend money on. 'Small businesses' fails.
questions.why: It feeds the site brief. A segment you can count, a place they gather, and what they already spend money on. "People who like bikes" is not answerable.
questions.example: Commuters in town with one bike each, no space to service it. Roughly 400 households within two miles.

questions.label: A3 The alternative
questions.question: What do they do today instead?
questions.help: At least three: a competitor, a spreadsheet, and doing nothing. Give the real cost of each. The free option is always one of them.
questions.why: The alternatives are what the pricing and category copy argue against. The free option is always one of them.
questions.example: Owning: storage, servicing, theft. Renting: per-day rates. A competing workshop: turnaround time.

questions.label: A4 The problem in their words
questions.question: What do they actually say the problem is?
questions.help: Two or three short quotes with a source. Not your summary. If there are none, write TBC and say so.
questions.why: Real quotes, not your summary. If you have none yet, that is a fact about the brand, not a gap in the answer.
questions.example: "I just want it back before Saturday." — collect the words, not the feeling.
questions.tbcHint: No customer conversations yet? Mark TBC. Interviews belong to the first four weeks.

questions.label: B1 The promise
questions.question: What changes for them, by when, and through what mechanism?
questions.help: Outcome + mechanism + timeframe. The mechanism must be a real feature. No 'seamless', 'world-class', 'revolutionary'.
questions.why: The promise is what changes for the visitor, by when, and through what mechanism. Tone words here are answering the wrong slot — tone belongs in C1 Voice.
questions.example: Bike collected by 9am, serviced and returned the same day. — outcome + mechanism + timeframe, no tone words.

questions.label: B2 Proof — exists now
questions.question: What can you show today?
questions.help: One per line. 'No customers yet' is a valid entry and must appear if true.
questions.why: What exists today. "No site yet" is a valid entry and must appear if true.

questions.label: B2 Proof — earnable in 90 days
questions.question: What could you honestly earn within ninety days?
questions.why: What you could honestly earn in ninety days. Nothing stated, nothing to record.
questions.tbcHint: No plan yet? Mark TBC rather than guess a number.

questions.label: B2 Proof — never claim
questions.question: What must never be claimed, by you or an agent writing for you?
questions.why: Agents and designers writing beside you must never claim these. This list is the only thing standing between copy and a fabricated claim.
questions.example: No testimonials from people we have not asked. No 5-star ratings that came from nowhere.

questions.label: B3 The offer
questions.question: What exactly do they buy, at what price, with what included and excluded, and what happens if it does not work?
questions.help: Quote the authoritative price. Never invent a trial length or a free tier; use TBC.
questions.why: The nav labels ("Hire", "Repairs"), the CTA text and the pricing page all come from this one slot. Quote the real price, or write TBC.
questions.example: Repair service from £19. Hire from £8/day. Includes lock and lights; excludes helmets.

questions.label: B4 The category
questions.question: What shelf is it on, and what is the comparison set?
questions.help: 'X for Y' in one line, plus the two or three products a buyer will compare it with.
questions.why: The category is what the buyer compares you to, so "X for Y" names the shelf.
questions.example: The local workshop alternative to a big-box online retailer.

questions.label: B5 The enemy
questions.question: What practice or status quo is this against?
questions.help: Not a named competitor. Paper cards, the group chat, the spreadsheet, the agency retainer.
questions.why: What you are against, that is not a person. It shapes the tone of the site copy and the heading voice.
questions.example: The council bike shed. The spreadsheet of repairs. The scroll past a competitor who would charge more for less.

questions.label: C1 Voice — five rules
questions.question: Five rules that make a sentence sound like this brand.
questions.help: Each must be checkable by reading a sentence aloud. One per line.
questions.why: These are the checkable voice rules an agent obeys before writing the first paragraph. Each one must be checkable by reading a sentence aloud.
questions.example: Second person, active voice. Name the reader. One idea per sentence. No weak hedges.

questions.label: C1 Voice — banned words
questions.question: Five words or phrases this brand never uses.
questions.why: These are the words your copy agent must refuse. Five is a workable number.

questions.label: C1 Voice — keeper lines
questions.question: Three lines already written and approved that show the voice.
questions.help: Approved, not newly written.
questions.why: Three approved lines that show the voice, not new lines written to fill the slot.
questions.tbcHint: Nothing approved yet? Mark TBC — inventing a keeper line defeats the slot.

questions.label: C2 Economics
questions.question: Price, margin, the most you can pay to acquire a customer, and how many you can serve.
questions.help: Show the arithmetic. Break-even count, intake cap, hours available.
questions.why: Price, margin, the most you can pay to acquire a customer — this sets whether the site is a booking site or a brochure, and what the performance budget is.
questions.tbcHint: Late? Mark TBC and note it as a gap. The site can be designed around the gaps.

questions.label: C3 The one motion
questions.question: Which single motion for the next four weeks — to whom, saying what, at what cadence, with what number says stop?
questions.help: One motion, not three. A named list, a first sentence, a date, a number and a kill rule.
questions.why: One motion for four weeks. The home page and the first email are built around it.
questions.example: Collect 20 booking requests via one flyer and one landing page. Kill rule: fewer than 5 in a week.
questions.tbcHint: Not decided yet? Mark TBC — do not assign a motion from the interview chair.

questions.label: V1 Logo
questions.question: What is the mark, the wordmark, and their lockups — with three misuses?
questions.help: Name the files or paths if they exist. If there is only a wordmark, say that.
questions.why: The mark, the wordmark, and their lockups feed the assets document. Naming what does not exist is as useful as naming what does.
questions.example: Wordmark only, set in the display face. No symbol yet. Misuse: against dark green, stretched.

questions.label: V2 Colour — paper
questions.question: What is the page colour?
questions.help: A hex value. This is the base everything is read against.
questions.why: The page base colour. Everything is read against it, so it starts the contrast table.

questions.label: V2 Colour — ink
questions.question: What is the primary text colour?
questions.why: Primary text colour. This is the second pair entered into contrast.

questions.label: V2 Colour — accent
questions.question: What is the one accent, and what is it allowed to do?
questions.help: Hex plus a limit: links only, one CTA per screen, etc.
questions.placeholder: #a4452e — CTA fills only, never body text
questions.why: One accent, and where it is permitted. "CTA fills only" is a statement about spending, not decoration.
questions.example: #a4452e — CTA fills and headings; never body text.

questions.label: V2 Colour — surface
questions.question: What is the card or raised surface colour?
questions.why: Card and raised-surface colour. This is where two more contrast pairs come from (ink, accent on surface).
questions.tbcHint: No colour yet? Mark TBC. The contrast table skips it until you have one.

questions.label: V3 Type — display
questions.question: Which face carries display, at what role, and is it licensed?
questions.help: Name the family and the licence. If it cannot be identified, describe the voice — never invent a name.
questions.why: The face that carries display at scale. Named from a file, a licence, or a pairing chosen below. If you cannot identify it, describe the voice.

questions.label: V3 Type — body
questions.question: Which face carries reading text, and at what size and measure?
questions.why: The reading face. It sets the measure and the tone of paragraphs across the site.

questions.label: V3 Type — UI and labels
questions.question: Which face carries nav, labels and buttons?
questions.why: The lábel face for nav, buttons, tags.

questions.label: V4 Imagery
questions.question: What is photographed or illustrated, in what treatment, and what is never shown?
questions.help: Name the source. Never claim photography you do not have.
questions.why: What is photographed or illustrated, in what treatment, and what is never shown. Nothing is invented later; this is the assets document.
questions.example: Action riding photos, in weather and at odd angles. Never: posed catalog people not on a bike.

questions.label: V5 Layout signatures
questions.question: What recurs on every page — grid, section rhythm, the one device?
questions.why: What recurs on every page of the site. Device and behaviour, not a subject. "Bicycle" is a subject; "one CTA per viewport, photo leads every section" is a signature.
questions.example: One CTA per viewport. A photo leads every section. Wide margins, narrow text column.

questions.label: V6 Motion
questions.question: What moves, what never moves, and what happens with reduced motion?
questions.why: What moves, what never moves, and what happens with reduced motion on.
questions.example: Page transitions only, 200–520ms; nothing loops. Reduced motion removes all of it.

questions.label: V7 Texture and detail
questions.question: Grain, rules, radii, icon style — what are the small recurring decisions?
questions.why: Small recurring decisions: grain, radii, rules, icon style. They make the site recognisable at 5% scale.
questions.example: Grain at 3.5%, 16px radius, hairline rules, no drop shadows on text.

questions.label: V8 Forbidden territory
questions.question: What would make this look like someone else?
questions.help: The clichés of the category, the competitor's signature, the trend you refuse. One per line.
questions.why: What would make this look like someone else. Checked before the build; the more concrete, the easier to say no at build time.
questions.example: Neon gradients. A blue-purple hero. Three equal cards. Anything the top-3 competitors already are.

questions.label: D1 Decision one
questions.question: First decision that makes the next direction specific.
questions.placeholder: Lora at 64px for the statement, not the wordmark
questions.why: Decision one of the direction. It names what the next design does, so the interview is not writing the design for you.
questions.example: Lora at 64px for the statement, Arco only for the wordmark.

questions.label: D1 Decision two
questions.question: Second decision.
questions.why: Decision two.

questions.label: D1 Decision three
questions.question: Third decision.
questions.why: Decision three.

questions.label: D1 Refusal
questions.question: What does this direction refuse to do?
questions.help: A decision with no refusal drifts back to the category default.
questions.why: What the direction refuses. A decision with no refusal drifts back to the category default.

questions.label: D2 Dials
questions.question: Score each dial now and where it should be.
questions.help: 1–5. The gap is the brief for the visual work.
questions.why: Current = the site you have today (leave unchecked pre-launch); target = where the brand should go. The gap is the brief for the visual work.

fontPairings.name: Editorial warmth
fontPairings.rationale: A high-contrast serif display over a reading serif. The UI stays quiet so the words carry the page.

fontPairings.name: Modern minimal
fontPairings.rationale: One serif moment, one neutral sans for everything else. Reads as considered rather than decorated.

fontPairings.name: Swiss technical
fontPairings.rationale: A grotesk with a mechanical body and mono for labels. Precise, systematic, no warmth claimed.

fontPairings.name: Publication
fontPairings.rationale: A text-first serif for headlines, a civic sans for body and chrome. Built to survive long reading.

fontPairings.name: Playful editorial
fontPairings.rationale: An expressive display face against a calm reading serif. One wink, not a clown.

fontPairings.name: Quiet luxe
fontPairings.rationale: Thin high-contrast display, geometric body, generous space. Expensive because it is quiet.
